correctness.rationale: For Q_d every edge has 2(d-1) adjacent edges. With exactly two colors, the strong-majority rule forces their signed sum to zero. If s_i(x)=s_i(x+e_i) is the direction-i edge sign and T(x)=sum_i s_i(x), the edge equation is T(x)+T(x+e_i)=2s_i(x), which on summation gives A_Q T=(2-d)T. Walsh characters diagonalize the cube adjacency, and eigenvalue 2-d is precisely the d-dimensional level-(d-1) eigenspace; hence T=sum_i a_i chi_[d]\{i} and s_i=a_i chi_[d]\{i}. Signs force all a_i to be +/-1, yielding exactly 2^d distinct feasible labelled-color patterns. Their construction satisfies balance. Translations act on a_i by J+I over F2, rank d for even d and d-1 for odd d; coordinate permutations preserve odd-d sign product. Therefore one named-color orbit for even d, two for odd d, and one after global color swap. I independently enumerated every sign assignment for Q2/Q3 and matched exactly 4/8 patterns. The general proof is spectral, not an extrapolation from these checks.

originality.rationale: Published general strong-majority edge-colouring papers establish existence and small-color bounds, including a three-color minimum-degree result, and the two-color cycle Q2 example. The submission identifies the *entire* two-color sign cube for all Q_d and its cube automorphism orbit structure. The equivalent zero-eigenspace intersection formulation does not follow just from the dimension of an eigenspace; the discrete sign rigidity argument is additional. No identified primary theorem covers the all-d hypercube sign-vector classification, subject to residual unindexed line-graph signed-nullvector literature.

value.rationale: The binary hypercube is a canonical highly symmetric graph family, and 2 colors is a sharp feasible strong-majority edge index despite large degrees. Exact classification of all optimal colorings and the parity-dependent orbit obstruction supplies genuinely more information than a two-color existence witness. The Walsh/line-graph spectral rigidity mechanism could be reused for related Cartesian-product balancing problems.
